section_map.title: Introduction
section_map.body:
Classification is a core architectural component of the Documentation Framework.

The Documentation Framework considers a document to be a coherent unit of knowledge with a defined purpose, permanent identity, standardized metadata, semantic classification, explicit relationships and a lifecycle.

Classification provides the architectural capability required to organize documents into meaningful semantic categories.

It enables documents to be organized independently of their physical representation and location.

---

section_map.title: Purpose
Scope
Architectural Position
section_map.body:
Classification belongs to the **Documentation Layer** of the Documentation Framework.

The Documentation Framework defines the Documentation Layer as the layer responsible for representing documentation as structured knowledge.

Conceptually:

```text

                    Documentation Framework
                    │
                    ├── Foundation
                    │
                    ├── Architecture
                    │
                    ├── Documentation Layer
                    │   │
                    │   ├── Metadata
                    │   ├── Document Identity
                    │   ├── Classification
                    │   └── Templates
                    │
                    ├── Governance Layer
                    │
                    ├── Discovery Layer
                    │
                    ├── Automation Layer
                    │
                    └── Integration Layer

```

Classification is therefore a peer component of Metadata and Document Identity within the Documentation Layer.

---

section_map.title: Architectural Role
section_map.body:
Classification provides semantic organization of documents.

Its role is distinct from the responsibilities of other Documentation Layer components.

Conceptually:

```text

                                      Document
                                         │
                ┌────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┐
                │                        │                        │
                ▼                        ▼                        ▼

             Metadata            Document Identity          Classification
                │                        │                        │
                │                        │                        │

            describes               identifies                organizes

```

Metadata describes the document.

Document Identity identifies the document.

Classification organizes the document semantically.

These responsibilities shall remain distinct.

---

section_map.title: Architectural Responsibility
section_map.body:
The Classification component is responsible for defining the semantic organization of documents.

Its responsibility includes the architectural mechanisms required to establish and maintain meaningful document categories.

Classification shall provide the semantic foundation required by higher-level capabilities that depend on document organization.

---

section_map.title: Classification as a Semantic Capability
Classification and Knowledge
Classification and Documents
section_map.body:
A document is the fundamental architectural unit of documentation.

Each document possesses semantic classification as one of its architectural characteristics.

Conceptually:

```text

                    Document
                    │
                    ├── Purpose
                    ├── Identity
                    ├── Metadata
                    ├── Classification
                    ├── Relationships
                    └── Lifecycle

```

Classification therefore describes one fundamental aspect of the document's place within the documentation architecture.

---

section_map.title: Responsibilities
Non-Responsibilities
Relationship with Metadata
section_map.body:
Metadata and Classification are complementary architectural capabilities.

Metadata provides standardized descriptive information about documents.

Classification provides semantic organization of documents.

The Metadata component explicitly identifies Classification as one of the architectural capabilities supported by Metadata.

Conceptually:

```text

                Metadata
                    │
                describes
                    │
                    ▼

                 Document
                    │
             is organized by
                    │
                    ▼

              Classification

```

Metadata therefore provides information required to represent Classification, while Classification owns the semantics of document classification.

---

section_map.title: Relationship with Document Identity
section_map.body:
Document Identity and Classification have different responsibilities.

Document Identity provides the permanent logical identity of a document.

Classification provides semantic organization.

The Document Identity component explicitly excludes document classification from its responsibilities.

Conceptually:

```text

                    Document
                    │
                    ├── Document Identity
                    │        └── identifies the document
                    │
                    └── Classification
                             └── organizes the document

```

A change in Classification shall therefore not constitute a change of Document Identity.

---

section_map.title: Relationship with Templates
section_map.body:
Templates belong to the Documentation Layer alongside Metadata, Document Identity and Classification.

Templates provide standardized document structures.

Classification provides semantic organization.

Conceptually:

```text

                 Template
                    │
            provides structure
                    │
                    ▼

                 Document
                    │
     receives semantic classification
                    │
                    ▼

              Classification

```

A template may represent Classification information, but it shall not become the semantic authority for classification.

---

section_map.title: Relationship with Governance
section_map.body:
Classification belongs to the Documentation Layer.

Governance belongs to a separate architectural layer responsible for controlling document lifecycle and governance.

Classification provides semantic information that Governance may consume.

Conceptually:

```text

           Documentation Layer
                    │
                    ▼

              Classification
                    │
      provides semantic information
                    │
                    ▼

             Governance Layer

```

Classification shall not assume governance responsibilities.

---

section_map.title: Relationship with Discovery
section_map.body:
Classification supports discovery because semantic categories provide meaningful ways of organizing and navigating documents.

The architectural concepts explicitly identify discovery as one of the capabilities supported by Classification.

Conceptually:

```text

                    Classification
                    │
                    ▼

                    Discovery
                        │
                        ├── Navigation
                        ├── Search
                        └── Knowledge Discovery

```

Classification therefore contributes semantic information to Discovery without implementing Discovery itself.

---

section_map.title: Relationship with Relationships
section_map.body:
Relationships provide explicit connections between architectural entities and enable architectural traceability.

Classification may participate in such relationships.

However, Classification and Relationships remain separate responsibilities.

Conceptually:

```text

              Classification
                    │
           may participate in
                    │ 
                    ▼

              Relationships

```

The Classification component defines classification semantics.

The Relationships component defines explicit connections between entities.

---

section_map.title: Relationship with Registry
section_map.body:
The Registry is the authoritative catalog of the Documentation Framework and maintains the existence and discoverability of architectural entities.

Classification may provide information that can be represented in the Registry.

However, Classification does not maintain the Registry.

Conceptually:

```text

              Classification
                    │
        classification information
                    │ 
                    ▼

                Registry

```

The Registry remains responsible for cataloging entities.

---

section_map.title: Relationship with Validation
section_map.body:
Classification requires validation to ensure that classification information conforms to the classification architecture.

Validation is a separate responsibility.

Conceptually:

```text

              Classification
                    │
       defines semantic conditions
                    │ 
                    ▼

                Validation
                    │
                verifies
                    │
                    ▼

        Classification Assignment

```

The Classification component therefore defines the semantic basis against which classification can be validated, while the Validation capability performs validation.

Detailed validation is deferred to **DF-CLS-007 — Classification Validation**.

---

section_map.title: Architectural Dependencies
section_map.body:
Classification belongs to the Documentation Layer and depends on the architectural foundations established by the Foundation and Architecture layers.

Conceptually:

```text

               Foundation
                    │
                    ▼

              Architecture
                    │
                    ▼

           Documentation Layer
                    │
                    ▼

              Classification

```

The framework's architectural dependency model establishes that higher layers consume services provided by lower layers while lower layers remain independent from higher-level implementation concerns.

---

section_map.title: Required Supporting Capabilities
section_map.body:
Classification relies on capabilities already established by the Documentation Layer, particularly:

- Metadata;
- Document Identity;
- Templates where classification information must be represented structurally.

Metadata is explicitly identified as an architectural support capability for Classification.

Classification shall not duplicate these capabilities.

---

section_map.title: Architectural Boundaries
section_map.body:
The Classification component has the following architectural boundaries:

```text

                    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │              Classification             │
                    │                                         │
                    │  Classification Concepts                │
                    │  Classification Model                   │
                    │  Classification Elements                │
                    │  Classification Schema                  │
                    │  Classification Lifecycle               │
                    │  Classification Validation              │
                    │  Classification Governance              │
                    │  Classification Relationships           │
                    │  Classification Constraints             │
                    │  Classification Extensibility           │
                    │  Classification Best Practices          │
                    │  Classification Dictionary              │
                    │  Classification Specification           │
                    │  Classification Examples                │
                    │                                         │
                    └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

The component boundary encompasses the semantic architecture of classification.

It does not encompass physical document management.

---

section_map.title: Architectural Independence
Modularity
section_map.body:
Classification is an independent architectural component.

The framework architecture defines its components as having clearly defined responsibilities and explicit relationships with other components.

Classification shall therefore evolve independently while preserving its established architectural contracts with other components.

---

section_map.title: Separation of Responsibilities
Knowledge Orientation
section_map.body:
Classification shall be oriented toward knowledge organization rather than file organization.

The architectural model treats documentation as structured knowledge rather than a collection of independent files.

Therefore:

```text

                Knowledge
                    │
                    ▼

              Documentation
                    │
                    ▼

                 Document
                    │
                    ▼

              Classification

```

Classification contributes to the organization and discoverability of that knowledge.

---

section_map.title: Traceability
section_map.body:
Classification shall support architectural traceability.

Classification information must remain explicitly associated with the document to which it applies.

Changes to classification shall therefore remain distinguishable from changes to:

- Document Identity;
- document content;
- physical location.

This is consistent with the framework's emphasis on explicit architectural relationships and traceability.

---

section_map.title: Extensibility
section_map.body:
The Classification architecture shall support controlled evolution.

The framework architecture is explicitly extensible and allows new components and capabilities to be introduced without modifying existing architectural foundations.

Classification shall therefore allow its semantic model to evolve while preserving existing classification semantics.

Detailed extensibility is deferred to **DF-CLS-011 — Classification Extensibility**.

---

section_map.title: Architectural Evolution
section_map.body:
Classification shall evolve incrementally.

The Documentation Framework roadmap establishes incremental evolution as an architectural principle and states that components evolve independently.

The Classification component therefore follows the progression defined by Milestone M6:


section_map.title: Architectural Principles
Architectural Characteristics
section_map.body: Classification shall exhibit the following characteristics:

section_map.title: Modular
section_map.body: Classification is a distinct architectural component.

section_map.title: Layered
section_map.body: Classification belongs to the Documentation Layer.

section_map.title: Traceable
section_map.body: Classification information and its evolution remain explicitly represented.

section_map.title: Extensible
section_map.body: The classification model may evolve without violating the architectural foundation.

section_map.title: Technology Independent
section_map.body: Classification does not depend on storage, repository or implementation technology.

section_map.title: Knowledge-Oriented
section_map.body:
Classification organizes documentation as structured knowledge.

These characteristics correspond to the established characteristics of the Documentation Framework architecture.

---

section_map.title: Architectural Model
section_map.body:
At the architectural level, Classification can be represented as:

```text

                         Documentation Framework
                                    │
                                    ▼

                           Documentation Layer
                                    │
            ┌───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┐
            │                       │                       │
            ▼                       ▼                       ▼

        Metadata            Document Identity         Classification
            │                       │                       │
            │                       │                       │
            └───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┘
                                    │
                                    ▼

                                 Document

```

Each component contributes a distinct capability to the representation of a document.

---

section_map.title: Component Interaction Model
section_map.body:
The principal architectural interactions can be summarized as:

```text

                           ┌──────────────┐
                           │   Metadata   │
                           └──────┬───────┘
                                  │
                                  ▼

                          ┌────────────────┐
                          │ Classification │
                          └───────┬────────┘
                                  │
                 ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
                 │                │                │
                 ▼                ▼                ▼

            Governance        Discovery        Validation
                 │                │                │
                 └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                                  │
                                  ▼

                               Document

```

The diagram represents architectural interaction, not implementation dependency.

---

section_map.title: Architectural Authority
section_map.body:
Classification is the semantic authority for document classification.

Other components may consume classification information, but they shall not independently redefine its meaning.

Conceptually:

```text

              Classification
                    │
            semantic authority
                    │ 
                    ▼

        Classification Information
                    │
                    ├── Metadata
                    ├── Governance
                    ├── Discovery
                    ├── Registry
                    └── Automation

```

This supports the framework principle of a Single Source of Truth.

---

section_map.title: Architectural Constraints
section_map.body:
The Classification architecture establishes the following high-level constraints:

- Classification shall remain within the Documentation Layer.
- Classification shall remain semantically independent from physical document location.
- Classification shall remain distinct from Document Identity.
- Classification shall remain distinct from general Metadata responsibilities.
- Classification shall not assume Governance responsibilities.
- Classification shall not assume Discovery responsibilities.
- Classification shall not assume Registry responsibilities.
- Classification shall remain technology independent.
- Classification evolution shall preserve architectural compatibility.

Detailed classification constraints are deferred to **DF-CLS-010 — Classification Constraints**.

# 5. Scope

The Documentation Framework is intended to document any knowledge-oriented project.

Typical applications include.

* Software Systems
* Frameworks
* Enterprise Architecture
* Research Projects
* Engineering Processes
* Organizational Knowledge
* Technical Standards

The framework is domain-independent.

---

# 6. Canonical Documentation

Framework documentation comprises complementary normalized documents and functional files. The received Version 1.0 described META Documentation, Templates, Documentation Standards, Naming Conventions, Documentation Workflow, Architectural Documentation and Supporting Reference Documents as families. That list is preserved here as historical subject/role vocabulary, not the current Family enumeration or a component register.

For normalized documents, Family identifies the canonical component or the explicitly scoped non-component documentary area in §10. Type identifies primary responsibility under §8. A title, topic, allocation series or directory does not by itself define either field.

Every file named **README.md**, **CHANGELOG.md** or **ArchitecturalMilestones.md**, at any location, is a non-normalized functional file. Normalization does not require Document ID, Family, Type, Component, Version, Revision, Status or Baseline for these files, and does not rename them into an ID-based series. Their content, references, inventory and SHA-256 evidence remain reviewable. CHANGELOG and Milestones retain their own record identifiers, dates and state conventions.

Authority as a normative or informative source requires an explicit applicable declaration and evidence. Presence in the corpus, Type=Reference, a directory name or this Manifest's entry-point role does not approve a working edition, publish it or assign it to a Baseline.

---

# 8. Interpretation Rules

Documents complement one another through explicit responsibility contracts. Each document has one primary responsibility; domain owners define the concepts within their scope. Consumers, summaries and projections reference those definitions rather than create competing authorities.

For every normalized document, Type uses exactly one of the following values, according to its primary responsibility.

| Type | Primary responsibility |
|---|---|
| Architecture | Foundations, principles, concepts, conceptual models and architectural decisions. |
| Structure | Organization, composition, schemas, structural relationships, restrictions and element catalogs. |
| Behavior | Processes, lifecycle, validation, governance, extensibility and planned evolution. |
| Reference | Consultation, terminology, consolidated specifications, examples, recommendations and historical records. |

There are no Foundation or Architecture exceptions and no additional Base/Core Type values. Family, Type, optional defined Class, component membership, structural allocation and permanent document identity are distinct dimensions. Physical placement does not determine responsibility.

Templates defines representation structures; its documents may have different Types according to responsibility. A Reference document may be normative or informative under its explicit declaration; Type alone establishes neither status nor authority.

Apply the functional-file exclusion in §6 before normalization. A responsibility principle may still guide those files' content without imposing a normalized header.

---

# 12. Evolution Policy

The Documentation Framework may evolve through new document roles and content, refined methodologies, additional Templates, new explicitly defined components and improved architectural organization.

Such additions use the four current Type values in §8. The received phrase “new document types” does not authorize an additional Type value. A future change to the classification contract requires an explicit governed decision, compatibility assessment and coordinated update of responsible definitions and consumers before the new contract is applied.

Preserve established architectural principles and permanent identities. Compatible clarifications, compatible additions and incompatible convention changes have distinct edition consequences under the Review Policy. Version, Revision, lifecycle Status and collective Baseline are separate dimensions.

An edited working successor starts Draft with Baseline Not assigned. Review, validation, approval, publication and selection into an immutable Baseline are separate evidenced events. Editing or passing a scoped check does not create approval or membership. Historical approved editions and snapshots remain preserved; later working successors do not retarget them.

This successor changes the previously permitted open-ended classification and unscoped interpretation convention. It therefore uses Version 2.0 Revision 1. No historical Revision 0 is inferred. Other domain sources require their scheduled reconciliation; this local update does not complete that rollout.

---

# 1. The Origin of the Need

---

## 1.1. Introduction

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

This document constitutes the chronological record of the research that led to the emergence of the **Documentation Framework**.

Unlike a technical specification, this journal is not intended to describe the final architecture of the system.

Its purpose is to preserve the discovery process.

The questions.

The hypotheses.

The experiments.

The decisions.

And, above all, the reasoning that led to the architecture currently proposed.

As happened with the VisualEngine, most of the solutions described here were not designed in advance.

They were discovered progressively.

**Current interpretation note.** The word chronological describes the received narrative progression. Dates and experiment evidence are not supplied; the actual dated UPDATE event is separate in §12.21. Current architectural definitions belong to their owner sources (§12.20), not to historical research conclusions.

---

## 1.2. The Context

The Documentation Framework did not originate as an independent project.

It was born during the development of the **VisualEngine**.

Initially, there was only the need to organize some technical documentation.

Nothing more.

The first documents were relatively simple.

* README;
* personal notes;
* task lists;
* small architecture documents.

Each document was created independently.

Without any common structure.

---

## 1.3. The Initial Problem

As the number of documents increased, difficulties began to emerge.

For example.

* duplicated documents;
* different formats;
* lack of conventions;
* inconsistent versions;
* contradictory information;
* difficulty locating knowledge.

The problem still seemed small.

But it was beginning to repeat itself.

---

## 1.4. The First Observation

It quickly became apparent that writing documentation was very different from maintaining documentation.

Creating a document is relatively simple.

Keeping it up to date for months or years proved to be significantly more difficult.

A question then began to emerge.

**Why does documentation degrade so quickly?**

---

## 1.5. Documentation as Code

One of the first ideas was to treat documentation in a manner similar to source code.

Source code has.

* structure;
* conventions;
* organization;
* review;
* evolution.

Why not apply the same principles to documentation?

This question would accompany the entire research process.

---

## 1.6. The Problem Was Not Markdown

Initially, it was believed that the main limitation lay in the language being used.

Perhaps Markdown was too simple.

Perhaps another technology was required.

However.

After several experiments, it became evident that the problem was not the syntax.

Markdown proved to be sufficiently expressive.

The difficulty existed at another level.

---

## 1.7. The Lack of Structure

After analysing several projects, a common pattern became evident.

Most documentation was organised solely through directories.

For example.

<!-- original-section-view: 1.7 -->
**Previously unnamed view in §1.7 — Historical file-list example.**

Physical names; not normalized allocations or dependencies.

| Position | Received term |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | docs/ |
| 2 | README.md |
| 3 | Architecture.md |
| 4 | Design.md |
| 5 | Notes.md |
| 6 | Todo.md |
<!-- end-original-section-view -->

Although functional.

This organisation did not explain.

* the role of each document;
* the existing relationships;
* the relative importance;
* the approval status;
* the historical evolution.

The documents were merely files.

---

## 1.8. A Fundamental Question

During this phase, a particularly important question emerged.

**What is a document, really?**

Is it merely a Markdown file?

Or does it represent something more?

At the time, there was still no clear answer.

But this question would eventually transform the entire project.

---

## 1.9. The Value of Knowledge

Another important observation was the realization that different documents had very different values.

Some contained simple temporary notes.

Others described fundamental architectural decisions.

However.

They were all treated in exactly the same way.

This lack of distinction was beginning to become problematic.

---

## 1.10. The Need for Identity

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

As the documentation grew, it also became difficult to reference documents consistently.

Names varied.

Titles changed.

Files were frequently reorganised.

The idea then began to emerge of assigning each document its own identity.

Not merely a name.

But a stable identifier.

This idea would be developed later.

**Current interpretation note.** Permanent identity is the logical key of a normalized document. Functional files are outside normalization scope; the current rule is stated in §4.15. Historical aspirations for every document do not allocate IDs to README files.

---

## 1.11. The Natural Evolution

Up to this point, the evolution can be summarised as follows.

<!-- original-section-view: 1.11 -->
**Previously unnamed view in §1.11 — Narrated emergence sequence.**

Presentation order; no verified dates, execution order or dependency chain.

| Position | Received term |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Notes |
| 2 | Documents |
| 3 | Document Collection |
| 4 | Need for Organization |
<!-- end-original-section-view -->

Although simple.

This sequence represented the true birth of the Documentation Framework.

---

## 1.12.  An Important Discovery

During this phase, it became evident that the problem was not writing documentation.

The real problem was managing knowledge.

Documentation was merely the physical representation of that knowledge.

This distinction proved to be extremely important.

---

## 1.13.  Initial Hypotheses

Several possibilities were then considered.

* standardising file names;
* creating templates;
* defining conventions;
* organising directories;
* creating indexes.

All these solutions helped.

But none completely solved the problem.

---

## 1.14.  The First Framework Idea

It was precisely at this point that a different hypothesis emerged.

Instead of producing documents alone.

Perhaps it would be possible to build an infrastructure for documentation.

An infrastructure that defined.

* rules;
* conventions;
* structure;
* evolution.

The concept of a Documentation Framework did not yet exist.

But the idea was beginning to take shape.

---

## 1.15.  Research Status

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

At the end of this first phase, several important conclusions had already been reached.

* Markdown was adequate.
* The problem was not technological.
* The problem was structural.
* Documentation represents knowledge.
* Knowledge requires organisation.
* Documents should possess identity.

These observations would serve as the foundation for all subsequent research.

**Current interpretation note.** Permanent identity is the logical key of a normalized document. Functional files are outside normalization scope; the current rule is stated in §4.15. Historical aspirations for every document do not allocate IDs to README files.

---

## 1.16.  Next Steps

The next stage would consist of finding a way to standardise documents.

Not merely through rules.

But through a common structure.

This research would lead to the emergence of the first **Templates**, marking the true beginning of document standardisation.

---

## 1.17.  Conclusion

The Documentation Framework was born from an extremely simple problem.

The difficulty of maintaining coherent documentation throughout the evolution of a project.

However, it quickly became clear that the issue went far beyond the organisation of Markdown files.

The real challenge was understanding how to structure knowledge in a consistent, evolutionary and reusable manner.

It was this change in perspective that gave rise to the research described in the following parts of this journal.

---

# 4. Document Identity

---

## 4.1. Introduction

The discovery of **Metadata** solved an important problem.

Documents came to possess their own properties.

However, a new difficulty quickly emerged.

How can a document be permanently identified?

For some time, only file names were used.

But this approach quickly revealed several limitations.

It was precisely from this need that the concept of **Document Identity** was born.

---

## 4.2. The Problem

The first documents were identified solely by their file names.

For example.

<!-- view: id1 -->
**View id1 — Historical physical-name examples.**

Names, not permanent ID allocations; functional exclusions apply.

| Position | Received term |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Architecture.md |
| 2 | Design.md |
| 3 | README.md |
| 4 | Notes.md |
<!-- end-view -->

This solution appeared to be sufficient.

But difficulties soon emerged.

---

## 4.3. Names Change

Throughout the evolution of a project, it is perfectly normal to change.

* titles;
* file names;
* directory locations.

Consequently.

A document could completely change its name.

While continuing to represent exactly the same knowledge.

Identity could not depend on the name.

---

## 4.4. The Document as an Entity

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

During this phase, an important analogy began to emerge.

In programming.

An object has identity.

Even if its state changes.

A document should likewise have a permanent identity.

Regardless of.

* its version;
* its title;
* its location;
* its content.

This idea profoundly changed the document architecture.

**Current interpretation note.** Ordinary rename, relocation, reclassification or edition evolution can retain logical identity. A semantic split/merge requires an explicit retained/new identity and provenance decision; it is not automatically the same entity. Repository/domain migration also requires scope assessment. No new identity is allocated in this UPDATE.

---

## 4.5. The First Identifier

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

The first proposal consisted of assigning a simple code to each document.

For example.

<!-- view: id2 -->
**View id2 — Historical identifier proposal.**

Received DOC syntax preserved; not current DF operational syntax.

| Position | Received term |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | DOC-001 |
| 2 | DOC-002 |
| 3 | DOC-003 |
<!-- end-view -->

Although this partially solved the problem.

It quickly revealed a limitation.

The identifier conveyed no meaning.

**Current interpretation note.** DOC and META-Family/Type codes are retained historical proposals, not current operational syntax. The adopted corpus format is DF-SSS-NNN: registered three-letter uppercase allocation series and positive 001–999, unique within the DF domain. Series are stable namespaces, not mutable Family/Type; reclassification does not recalculate a valid ID. Allocation requires collision/history checks; no 000/README ID or general migration is performed. DF-FND-002 remains unchanged.

---

## 4.6. The Search for Semantics

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

A new question then emerged.

Could the identifier itself contain information?

For example.

* family;
* type;
* number.

In this way.

The identifier would no longer be just a number.

It would also communicate context.

**Current interpretation note.** DOC and META-Family/Type codes are retained historical proposals, not current operational syntax. Series are stable namespaces, not mutable Family/Type; reclassification does not recalculate a valid ID. Allocation requires collision/history checks; no 000/README ID or general migration is performed. DF-FND-002 remains unchanged.

## 4.8. The Concept of Type

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

It quickly became apparent that Family alone was still too generic.

Within the same Family there were very different documents.

A second level of classification then began to emerge.

The **Type**.

## 4.9. Numbering

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

Once Family and Type had been defined.

Only one element remained.

Distinguishing documents belonging to the same category.

Conceptually.

## 4.10. The Discovery of Classes

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

During practical use, another need emerged.

Not all documents fulfil the same role.

Others merely record research.

Others describe architecture.

## 4.11. Identity Becomes Permanent

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

A particularly important decision was made during this phase.

The identifier must never change.

Even if.

* the title is modified;
* the content evolves;
* the document is reorganised.

This principle brought documents significantly closer to software entities.

No new identity is allocated in this UPDATE.

From physical location.

A document may be moved between directories.

Yet it continues to represent exactly the same document.

This separation proved essential for the future evolution of the framework.

**Current interpretation note.** Ordinary rename, relocation, reclassification or edition evolution can retain logical identity. A semantic split/merge requires an explicit retained/new identity and provenance decision; it is not automatically the same entity. Repository/domain migration also requires scope assessment. No new identity is allocated in this UPDATE.

---

## 4.13. Metadata Evolves

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

With the introduction of identifiers.

Metadata also became richer.

For example.

<!-- view: id6 -->
**View id6 — Historical descriptor field list.**

Fields are descriptors, not identity segments; no Class/catalog is prescribed.

| Position | Received term |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Document ID |
| 2 | Family |
| 3 | Type |
| 4 | Class |
| 5 | Version |
| 6 | Revision |
| 7 | Status |
| 8 | Baseline |
<!-- end-view -->

Metadata was no longer merely administrative.

It progressively came to represent the document structure itself.

**Current interpretation note.** The field list describes the historical header experiment, not the semantic composition of permanent identity or a mandatory current schema. Descriptor applicability belongs to Dictionary/Schema/Profile contracts and the corresponding domain owners.

---

## 4.14. The Document as an Architectural Object

At this stage, one particularly important idea became evident.

A document was no longer considered merely a file.

It came to represent an architectural object.

With.

* identity;
* properties;
* state;
* lifecycle.

This conceptual change laid the foundation for almost all subsequent evolution of the Documentation Framework.

---

## 4.15. Research Status

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

At the end of this phase, several fundamental principles had been established.

* Every document has a permanent identity.
* Identity does not depend on the name.
* Identity does not depend on the location.
* Family organises knowledge.
* Type specialises the Family.
* Class defines the nature of the document.
* The identifier must remain stable throughout the entire lifecycle.

These decisions would remain virtually unchanged until the current architecture.

**Current interpretation note.** Historical Family/Type/Class and every-document claims are not the current classification/identity contract. Family denotes the canonical component or scoped documentary area (Foundation here); Type uses the uniform four values Architecture, Structure, Behavior, Reference. Stable allocation series are independent of classification. Every README.md, CHANGELOG.md and ArchitecturalMilestones.md at any location is non-normalized: no normalized ID/header/classification or ID-based renaming is required; content/reference/hash checks still apply.

---

## 4.16. Next Steps

As identifiers matured, an unexpected observation emerged.

Some documents did not describe the project.

They described the documentation itself.

In other words.

There were documents whose domain was the Documentation Framework itself.

This discovery would lead directly to the emergence of a new document category.

The **META Documents**.

---

## 4.17. Conclusion

The formalisation of document identity represented one of the most important milestones in the evolution of the Documentation Framework.

By definitively separating identity, content, and location, documents came to possess an existence of their own within the architecture.

This decision made it possible to introduce mechanisms for traceability, automation, and controlled evolution that would have been impossible using file names alone.

It was precisely upon this foundation that the next stage of the research emerged: the creation of **META Documents**, whose purpose was no longer to describe a project, but to describe the documentation system itself.

---

# 5. The Birth of META Documents

---

## 5.1. Introduction

The formalisation of document identity led to an unexpected discovery.

As the number of documents increased, a very particular type of documentation began to emerge.

These documents did not describe the VisualEngine.

Nor algorithms.

Nor components.

Nor architecture.

They described the documentation itself.

It was precisely at this point that the concept of **META Documents** was born.

---

## 5.2. A Different Problem

Up to this stage, all documents had a relatively clear purpose.

They described.

* components;
* decisions;
* research;
* references.

However.

Questions of a completely different nature began to emerge.

For example.

* How should a document be identified?
* How should a Template evolve?
* Which Metadata is mandatory?
* How are two documents related?

These questions no longer belonged to the project domain.

They belonged to the documentation domain.

---

## 5.3. Documentation Becomes a Domain

A new hypothesis was then formulated.

Documentation should be considered a domain in its own right.

Just like.

* Finance;
* Artificial Intelligence;
* Robotics.

Documentation also has.

* entities;
* rules;
* concepts;
* processes.

This change in perspective proved to be decisive.

---

## 5.4. The First META Document

The initial solution consisted of creating a document dedicated exclusively to documentation rules.

Conceptually.

<!-- view: meta1 -->
**View meta1 — Historical documentation-rule association.**

Conceptual role, not a required component dependency.

| Position | Received term |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | META |
| 2 | Documentation Rules |
<!-- end-view -->

This document did not describe the project.

It described how the project should be documented.

---

## 5.5. A New Document Category

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

The need to distinguish these documents from all others quickly emerged.

A new Family was created.

<!-- view: meta2 -->
**View meta2 — Historical META grouping.**

Historical label, not current extra Type.

| Position | Received term |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | META |
<!-- end-view -->

This Family came to represent documents whose domain is the Documentation Framework itself.

It became one of the first Families to span the entire project.

**Current interpretation note.** META and META-DCL/REF/CON/WFL are historical labels/proposals. They do not add current Types or recalculate IDs. Current domain definitions are maintained by their responsible sources; corpus presence or an old label does not grant approval. The received all-documents-version example excludes functional-file normalization under the adopted scope.

---

## 5.6. Self-Reference

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

During this phase, an interesting question emerged.

Can a system document itself?

Initially, this idea seemed paradoxical.

But it quickly became apparent that there was no contradiction.

Provided that clear levels of abstraction were established.

META Documents do not document a specific document.

They document the rules used by all documents.

**Current interpretation note.** Self-description is a historical design objective. It does not prove every current decision is fully represented or all sources are coherent. Responsible-source definitions and traceable edition references remain necessary.

---

## 5.7. The Emergence of the First META Documents

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

Specialised documents then began to appear.

For example.

<!-- view: meta3 -->
**View meta3 — Historical META specialization list.**

Old proposal codes, not new/current ID allocations.

| Position | Received term |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | META-DCL |
| 2 | META-REF |
| 3 | META-CON |
| 4 | META-WFL |
<!-- end-view -->

Each had clearly defined responsibilities.

Together, they began to form a true documentation architecture.

**Current interpretation note.** META and META-DCL/REF/CON/WFL are historical labels/proposals. They do not add current Types or recalculate IDs. Current domain definitions are maintained by their responsible sources; corpus presence or an old label does not grant approval. The received all-documents-version example excludes functional-file normalization under the adopted scope.

---

## 5.8. From Convention to Specification

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

Until this point, many decisions were merely conventions.

With the introduction of META Documents, they became formalised.

For example.

A convention.

"All documents must have a version."

Became a formal rule.

Defined.

Documented.

Versioned.

And subject to evolution.

This change significantly increased the consistency of the framework.

**Current interpretation note.** META and META-DCL/REF/CON/WFL are historical labels/proposals. They do not add current Types or recalculate IDs. Current domain definitions are maintained by their responsible sources; corpus presence or an old label does not grant approval. The received all-documents-version example excludes functional-file normalization under the adopted scope.

---

## 5.9. Knowledge About Knowledge

A particularly interesting consequence was the realisation that META Documents represent a higher level of knowledge.

While an architecture document describes a system.

A META Document describes how that document should exist.

This level of abstraction brought the Documentation Framework closer to metamodeling.

---

## 5.10. Internal Organisation

As the number of META Documents grew, it became evident that they too required organisation.

Relationships between them then began to emerge.

For example.

<!-- view: meta4 -->
**View meta4 — Illustrative historical typed relations.**

Received Defines/Uses/Related to associations; Uses lacks a required-contract assertion.

| Source | Received relation | Target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| META-DCL | Defines | META-REF |
| META-REF | Uses (not scoped as mandatory) | META-CON |
| META-CON | Related to | META-WFL |
<!-- end-view -->

For the first time, the documentation itself had its own architecture.

---

## 5.11. The Evolution of Rules

Another important observation was the realisation that documentation rules also evolve.

Consequently.

META Documents also came to have.

* versions;
* revisions;
* history;
* states.

The framework thus began to document the evolution of its own rules.

---

## 5.12. A Self-Describing Architecture

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

It was precisely during this phase that an ambitious objective emerged.

The Documentation Framework should be capable of explaining itself.

Every documentation decision should be understandable by consulting the META Documents.

This objective would strongly influence all subsequent evolution.

**Current interpretation note.** Self-description is a historical design objective. It does not prove every current decision is fully represented or all sources are coherent. Responsible-source definitions and traceable edition references remain necessary.

---

## 5.13. The Limits of META

Despite the enormous progress achieved.

A philosophical question also began to emerge.

META Documents explain the rules.

But who explains why those rules change?

This question remained unanswered for some time.

It would later lead directly to integration with the **Change Management System**.

---

## 5.14. Research Status

At the end of this phase, several conclusions had been established.

* Documentation constitutes a domain in its own right.
* META Documents document that domain.
* Documentation rules must be formalised.
* META Documents have identity and a lifecycle.
* Documentation requires its own architecture.
* The framework must be capable of explaining its own rules.

These ideas marked an important turning point in the research.

---

## 5.15. Next Steps

With the META Documents consolidated, a new need emerged.

The documentation rules already existed.

But one essential problem remained unresolved.

How can the simultaneous evolution of dozens or hundreds of documents be controlled?

How can it be ensured that a collection of documents represents a coherent state of the documentation?

The answer would begin to emerge through the concepts of **Baseline**, **Document Versioning**, and **Controlled Revision**, which would become the subject of the next stage of the research.

---

## 5.16. Conclusion

The emergence of **META Documents** represented the definitive transition from an organised collection of documents to a true documentation framework.

Documentation ceased to be merely a means of communication.

It came to possess its own rules, its own architecture, and a formal set of documents responsible for defining its structure and evolution.

This was the moment when the Documentation Framework acquired its identity as an independent project, rather than remaining merely a collection of conventions associated with the VisualEngine.

---

# 6. Baselines and Document Versioning

---

## 6.1. Introduction

The creation of **META Documents** solved an important problem.

The documentation rules became formally defined.

However, a new difficulty quickly emerged.

Even with well-established rules, documentation continued to evolve continuously.

New documents were created.

Others were modified.

Some were removed.

The question therefore became different.

**How can it be ensured that a collection of documents represents a coherent state of the documentation?**

It was from this need that the concepts of **Baseline** and **Document Versioning** were born.

---

## 6.2. The Problem

For some time, each document evolved independently.

For example.

<!-- view: bl1 -->
**View bl1 — Illustrative mixed document Versions.**

Received example editions; no actual identified member selection.

| Received subject | Illustrative Version |
| --- | --- |
| Architecture | Version 2.1 |
| Documentation | Version 1.4 |
| Reference | Version 3.0 |
| Workflow | Version 1.2 |
<!-- end-view -->

Individually.

Each document made sense.

Together.

They did not always represent the same architecture.

---

## 6.3. The Discovery of Consistency

It quickly became apparent that the real problem was not the version of an individual document.

It was the consistency between multiple documents.

A significant change in one document could require updates to many others.

Evolution was no longer local.

It became systemic.

---

## 6.4. The Concept of Baseline

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

A new idea was then introduced.

Instead of considering documents individually.

A consistent collection of documents came to be considered.

This collection was named a **Baseline**.

Conceptually.

<!-- view: bl2 -->
**View bl2 — Historical snapshot grouping.**

Illustrative subject members; current inclusion requires exact immutable editions.

| Historical grouping | Illustrative subject |
| --- | --- |
| Baseline | Architecture |
| Baseline | Reference |
| Baseline | Workflow |
| Baseline | Templates |
| Baseline | Standards |
<!-- end-view -->

A Baseline represents a coherent state of knowledge.

**Current interpretation note.** The current DF Baseline synopsis selects immutable approved document editions by logical ID plus exact Version/Revision or equivalent, with relevant pinned relationship context and evidence. Snapshot identity, member identity, edition Status and explicit membership differ. A current path or header alone does not establish inclusion; changes do not retarget old members.

---

## 6.5. Baseline Is Not a Version

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

Initially, there was some tendency to confuse a Baseline with a version.

It quickly became clear that they are different concepts.

A version describes a document.

A Baseline describes a collection of documents.

This distinction became a fundamental principle.

**Current interpretation note.** The current DF Baseline synopsis selects immutable approved document editions by logical ID plus exact Version/Revision or equivalent, with relevant pinned relationship context and evidence. Snapshot identity, member identity, edition Status and explicit membership differ. A current path or header alone does not establish inclusion; changes do not retarget old members.

---

## 6.6. The Role of Revisions

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

During this phase, it also became evident that not all changes have the same significance.

Some correct errors.

Others fundamentally change the architecture.

A distinction therefore began to emerge between.

* Version;
* Revision.

A Version identifies a significant evolution.

A Revision represents small, backward-compatible changes.

**Current interpretation note.** The received small-change Revision interpretation is historical. Under the adopted policy, Version is major.minor: compatible clarification keeps Version, compatible additive contracts increment minor, incompatible contracts increment major and reset minor. Each changed finalized edition increments Revision monotonically across Version changes; absent Revision first becomes 1. Validation alone changes neither field. Actual change compatibility must be assessed, not inferred from text size.

---

## 6.7. Document Status

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

Another important discovery was the realisation that document evolution does not depend solely on the version.

It also depends on the status.

For example.

<!-- view: bl3 -->
**View bl3 — Historical state progression experiment.**

Sample order, not current complete transition permissions or automatic approval.

| Position | Received term |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Draft |
| 2 | Review |
| 3 | Approved |
| 4 | Deprecated |
| 5 | Archived |
<!-- end-view -->

The status came to represent the point in the lifecycle at which a document currently exists.

**Current interpretation note.** These are historical lifecycle experiments/state examples, not a universal current transition graph. States concern exact editions; an older Approved edition may coexist with a Draft successor. Applicable Governance owner policies determine transitions, eligibility and evidence. Review and validation do not automatically approve an edition.

---

## 6.8. The Collection Must Remain Consistent

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

An immediate consequence of this approach was the need to validate the entire documentation.

Whenever a document evolves.

A new question arises.

Is it still compatible with the current Baseline?

If not.

The Baseline must evolve.

Or the change must be postponed.

**Current interpretation note.** Approved snapshot selections remain immutable. A significant change may be prepared as a Draft successor without immediately creating a new Baseline or altering the old one. New snapshot selection requires applicable eligibility, consistency, approval and explicit inclusion decisions; it is neither automatic nor restricted to small increments by this journal.

---

## 6.9. The First Baseline

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

It was precisely during this phase that the project's first formal Baseline emerged.

Its objective was simple.

To represent a stable state of the documentation.

From that moment onwards.

New changes no longer modified that state directly.

Instead, they first passed through an evolution process.

**Current interpretation note.** The first-Baseline statement is a received historical assertion. No selection identity/date/member-edition record or approval evidence was supplied for that event; this UPDATE does not reconstruct or certify it.

---

## 6.10. The Concept of Freezing

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

Another important idea emerged naturally.

An approved Baseline must remain immutable.

New changes do not modify the existing Baseline.

They create a new Baseline.

This principle made it possible to preserve historical traceability.

**Current interpretation note.** Approved snapshot selections remain immutable. A significant change may be prepared as a Draft successor without immediately creating a new Baseline or altering the old one. New snapshot selection requires applicable eligibility, consistency, approval and explicit inclusion decisions; it is neither automatic nor restricted to small increments by this journal.

---

## 6.11. Incremental Evolution

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

The research also demonstrated that large changes are more difficult to control.

Consequently.

Baselines began to evolve incrementally.

Each new Baseline represents a small evolution relative to the previous one.

This model significantly simplified documentation management.

**Current interpretation note.** Approved snapshot selections remain immutable. A significant change may be prepared as a Draft successor without immediately creating a new Baseline or altering the old one. New snapshot selection requires applicable eligibility, consistency, approval and explicit inclusion decisions; it is neither automatic nor restricted to small increments by this journal.

---

## 6.12. The Impact on Metadata

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

Metadata evolved once again.

New fields became part of the document header.

For example.

<!-- view: bl4 -->
**View bl4 — Historical snapshot/edition descriptor list.**

Illustrative fields; snapshot identity, member edition and membership differ.

| Position | Received term |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Baseline |
| 2 | Version |
| 3 | Revision |
| 4 | Status |
| 5 | Last Updated |
<!-- end-view -->

The document now explicitly indicates the Baseline to which it belongs.

**Current interpretation note.** The current DF Baseline synopsis selects immutable approved document editions by logical ID plus exact Version/Revision or equivalent, with relevant pinned relationship context and evidence. Snapshot identity, member identity, edition Status and explicit membership differ. A current path or header alone does not establish inclusion; changes do not retarget old members.

---

## 6.13. Preparing for Automation

As Baselines and versions became established, a new possibility began to emerge.

Documentation validation could be automated.

For example.

A tool could verify.

* incompatible documents;
* inconsistent versions;
* invalid references;
* outdated documents.

This possibility brought the Documentation Framework closer to configuration engineering.

---

## 6.14. Research Status

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

At the end of this phase, several principles had been established.

* A Baseline represents a coherent state of the documentation.
* Baseline and Version are distinct concepts.
* Documents have their own lifecycle.
* Significant changes create new Baselines.
* Approved Baselines remain immutable.
* Documentation consistency became an architectural objective.

These decisions remained virtually unchanged throughout the subsequent phases.

**Current interpretation note.** Approved snapshot selections remain immutable. A significant change may be prepared as a Draft successor without immediately creating a new Baseline or altering the old one. New snapshot selection requires applicable eligibility, consistency, approval and explicit inclusion decisions; it is neither automatic nor restricted to small increments by this journal.

---

## 6.15. Next Steps

**Received research account — historical interpretation.**

The introduction of Baselines resolved the temporal consistency of the documentation.

However.

Another question still remained unanswered.

How can a document be located quickly?

How can all related documents be discovered?

How can the existing knowledge be navigated?

These questions would lead directly to the emergence of the **Document Registry**, responsible for the organisation, discovery, and traceability of the entire documentation asset.

**Current interpretation note.** The narrative assesses Baselines as solving temporal consistency. Current consistency depends on actual exact-edition selection and verification; an architectural idea alone is not evidence that the supplied corpus has been reconciled.

---

## 6.16. Conclusion

The introduction of the concepts of **Baseline** and **Document Versioning** represented one of the greatest advances of the Documentation Framework.

Documentation ceased to be regarded as a collection of independent files and came to be treated as a coherent system capable of representing stable states of knowledge over time.

This evolution naturally prepared the next stage of the research, where the focus would shift from the individual evolution of documents to the integrated management of the entire documentation collection through the **Document Registry**.

---

# 1. Before the Framework

---

## 1.1. Introduction

**Received phase account — historical interpretation.**

This timeline describes the historical evolution of the **Documentation Framework**, identifying the events that led to its creation and the major transformations that occurred throughout its development.

Unlike the *Research Journal*, which explains the process through which ideas were discovered, this document seeks to answer a different question.

**When did these changes occur, and how did they evolve over time?**

The timeline begins before the framework itself existed.

**Current interpretation note.** This is an undated relative phase narrative. Neither this timeline nor comparison with the Research Journal supplies independent calendar dates; current owner definitions are listed in §15.20.

---

## 1.2. Context

During the early stages of the VisualEngine development, no documentation system existed.

Documentation was created only when an immediate need arose.

It was common to find.

* personal notes;
* README files;
* small technical notes;
* experimental documents.

There was no overall organization.

---

## 1.3. Characteristics

During this phase.

The documentation exhibited several typical characteristics.

* lack of a uniform structure;
* absence of conventions;
* inconsistent naming;
* limited reuse;
* strong dependence on the author.

Each document was created independently.

---

## 1.4. Organization

The organization depended entirely on the directory structure.

For example.

<!-- original-section-view: 1.4 -->
**Previously unnamed view in §1.4 — Historical directory example.**

Physical directories; no normalized allocation or dependency.

| Position | Received term |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | docs/ |
| 2 | notes/ |
| 3 | temp/ |
| 4 | misc/ |
<!-- end-original-section-view -->

Directories were used only to separate files.

No semantic organization existed.

---

## 1.5. Observed Problems

As the project grew, several difficulties began to emerge.

Among them.

* duplicated information;
* contradictory documents;
* difficulty locating knowledge;
* lack of traceability;
* complex maintenance.

Initially, these problems appeared to be isolated.

Later, it became clear that they shared a common origin.

---

## 1.6. First Attempts

Small organizational initiatives then began to appear.

For example.

* using consistent titles;
* separating technical and functional documentation;
* creating dedicated directories.

These improvements partially simplified maintenance.

However, they did not solve the structural problem.

---

## 1.7. Documentation Remains Secondary

During this phase.

Documentation was regarded as a by-product of development.

The priority was the code.

Whenever time became limited.

Documentation was postponed.

This culture proved to be one of the main obstacles to future evolution.

---

## 1.8. Project Growth

As the VisualEngine increased in size.

The number of documents grew rapidly.

There was now.

* architectural documentation;
* technical documentation;
* experimental documentation;
* research documentation.

The diversity increased significantly.

---

## 1.9. The First Sign

It was precisely during this phase that the first important sign appeared.

The problems were no longer related to individual documents.

They became related to the documentation as a whole.

The challenge was no longer writing documents.

It was managing documentation.

---

## 1.10. A Change in Perspective

A new idea then began to emerge.

Perhaps documentation should be treated as a system.

Rather than merely as a collection of files.

Although still very immature.

This hypothesis would influence every subsequent stage of the framework's evolution.

---

## 1.11. Situation at the End of the Phase

At the end of this period.

The project presented the following situation.

* existing documentation;
* distributed knowledge;
* no documentation architecture;
* no formal standards;
* increasing maintenance difficulties.

Despite its limitations.

This phase proved to be extremely important.

It clearly demonstrated the need for a completely different approach.

---

## 1.12. Historical Milestone

**The first realization that documentation is an architectural problem rather than merely an editorial one.**

This conclusion represents the true starting point of the Documentation Framework's evolution.

---

## 1.13. Consequences

From this point onward.

The research no longer focused on producing better documents.

It began searching for a better system to produce, organize, and maintain documentation.

This change in objective marked the conceptual birth of the project.

---

## 1.14. Next Stage

With the problem now clearly identified.

The next stage would focus on the first attempts at standardization.

The first document models, writing conventions, and later the **Templates** would emerge, representing the first concrete step toward building the Documentation Framework.

---

## 1.15. Phase Summary

**Received phase account — historical interpretation.**

| Aspect | Status |
|---------|--------|
| Organization | Informal |
| Templates | Non-existent |
| Metadata | Non-existent |
| Document Identity | Non-existent |
| Workflow | Non-existent |
| Registry | Non-existent |
| Baselines | Non-existent |
| Document Relationships | Implicit |
| Documentation Architecture | Non-existent |

**Current interpretation note.** Summary labels are received narrative phase assessments, not document edition Status, a dated capability inventory or acceptance evidence. Operational/Complete/Stable/Consolidated labels do not certify current implementation. The tooling limits in §§13.9/14.12 remain part of the received account.

---

## 1.16. Conclusion

The period before the Documentation Framework was characterized by largely informal documentation, sufficient for small projects but incapable of supporting the architectural growth of the VisualEngine.

It was precisely the accumulation of these limitations that made the need for a dedicated documentation infrastructure evident.

Every evolution described in the following phases can be understood as a progressive response to the problems identified during this initial period.

---

# 4. Metadata Standardization

---

## 4.1. Introduction

**Received phase account — historical interpretation.**

The consolidation of Templates significantly improved the structural organization of the documentation.

However.

During their practical use, a recurring observation began to emerge.

Regardless of the document type, there was always a common set of information.

This information did not describe the knowledge itself.

It described the document.

It was precisely this discovery that led to the process of **Metadata standardization**.

**Current interpretation note.** Common-field and minimum-core assertions describe received experiments, not a complete current mandatory descriptor catalog. Every README.md, CHANGELOG.md and ArchitecturalMilestones.md at any location is non-normalized: no normalized ID/header, Family, Type, Component, Version, Revision, Status or Baseline is required. Content/reference/inventory/hash checks still apply. Dictionary defines descriptors, Schema organizes references, Profile supplies applicable constraints and Instance supplies values under one effective Profile; no element/catalog/Profile lifecycle records are allocated here.

---

## 4.2. Primary Objective

The objective was no longer simply to organize documents.

It also became necessary to organize the information about those documents.

This represented a significant conceptual evolution.

---

## 4.3. Repeated Information

**Received phase account — historical interpretation.**

After analyzing dozens of documents, it became evident that many elements were repeatedly present.

For example.

* author;
* version;
* date;
* language;
* status;
* project.

Although these elements appeared in nearly every document.

There was no consistent standard for them.

**Current interpretation note.** Common-field and minimum-core assertions describe received experiments, not a complete current mandatory descriptor catalog. Every README.md, CHANGELOG.md and ArchitecturalMilestones.md at any location is non-normalized: no normalized ID/header, Family, Type, Component, Version, Revision, Status or Baseline is required. Content/reference/inventory/hash checks still apply. Dictionary defines descriptors, Schema organizes references, Profile supplies applicable constraints and Instance supplies values under one effective Profile; no element/catalog/Profile lifecycle records are allocated here.

---

## 4.4. Initial Attempts

Initially.

Each Template began to include a small header.

For example.

<!-- view: ev4-1 -->
**View ev4-1 — Historical header experiment.**

Illustrative fields, not a current mandatory catalog.

| Position | Received term |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Title |
| 2 | Author |
| 3 | Version |
| 4 | Date |
<!-- end-view -->

This solution reduced some inconsistencies.

However, it quickly revealed new limitations.

---

## 4.5. The Need for Uniformity

**Received phase account — historical interpretation.**

A new concern then emerged.

Should every document use exactly the same fields?

Or should different Templates be allowed to define their own?

After several experiments.

A common minimum set of fields was identified.

This core gradually became mandatory.

**Current interpretation note.** Common-field and minimum-core assertions describe received experiments, not a complete current mandatory descriptor catalog. Every README.md, CHANGELOG.md and ArchitecturalMilestones.md at any location is non-normalized: no normalized ID/header, Family, Type, Component, Version, Revision, Status or Baseline is required. Content/reference/inventory/hash checks still apply. Dictionary defines descriptors, Schema organizes references, Profile supplies applicable constraints and Instance supplies values under one effective Profile; no element/catalog/Profile lifecycle records are allocated here.

---

## 4.6. The Metadata Concept

**Received phase account — historical interpretation.**

It was during this phase that the term **Metadata** began to be used systematically.

Metadata came to represent all the information that describes a document.

But does not belong to its content.

Document Identity owns the logical identity contract: Domain+Identifier identifies a normalized document independently of classification, content, filename, location, Version and Revision. Title is a mutable label, not an identity key.

## 2.11. Baselines

Baselines defines immutable, coherent snapshots of explicitly selected approved document editions. Each member references a document identity and an exact Version/Revision or equivalent immutable edition reference. A Baseline has its own identity and is not an individual document Version.

A new Draft successor does not change an earlier Baseline or inherit membership. Baselines is primarily allocated to Governance and contributes to the conceptual Preservation concern. Approval, selection and reproducibility evidence remain distinct.

---

## 3.11. Document Identity

<!-- end-view -->

Within this corpus, DF-SSS-NNN uses DF as the representation prefix for the Documentation Framework identity domain, a registered three-letter uppercase allocation series SSS and a positive three-digit number NNN (001–999). Series codes do not recalculate when current Family, Type or component membership changes. Existing FND/ARC/MTD/DID/CLS/TPL/RDM allocations remain stable; RVW is allocated for review artifacts. Equal numbers in different series are not full-ID collisions.

## 4.11. Baselines

Baselines references a coherent selection of approved immutable document editions. Policies establishes inclusion conditions; Workflow and Reviews provide applicable state/quality evidence; selection is explicit and independently recorded.

Editing or checking a document does not create a Baseline, confer approval or inherit prior membership. A prior approved edition may remain selected while its new working successor is Draft and unassigned. Baselines is primarily allocated to Governance while contributing to Preservation.

---

## 6.3. Baseline Concept

A Baseline is an independently identified immutable selection of coherent approved document editions. It is not an individual document Version and does not merely refer to whichever revision is current.

<!-- view: ab6-1 -->
**View ab6-1 — snapshot membership; references select immutable editions.**

| Baseline member | Selected edition |
| --- | --- |
| Document A identity | Exact Version/Revision or immutable equivalent. |
| Document B identity | Exact Version/Revision or immutable equivalent. |
| Membership | Explicit approved selection; not a reference to whichever edition is current. |
<!-- end-view -->

Membership selects document identity plus exact Version/Revision or an equivalent immutable edition reference. Reproducibility requires preservation of the selected content and relevant context; physical evidence may include a hash without prescribing a storage technology.

---

## 6.6. Inclusion Criteria

Inclusion requires policy-defined eligibility and an explicit selection record. The conceptual contract includes approval for the exact edition, valid descriptive information, consistent identity, verified relevant relationships and reproducible edition references.

Reviews/validation evidence does not replace approval or selection. The executing process records evidence under these contracts; this edition neither creates a new approved Baseline nor completes missing historical membership evidence.

---

## 8.11. Architectural Dependencies

A mandatory dependency identifies a consumer that requires a provider contract. Write its edge consumer→provider and record the contract, scope and justification. Conceptual refinement, documentary authority reference, data projection, navigation and chronological activity are separately typed relations.

<!-- view: ab8-5 -->
**View ab8-5 — selected intended contract dependencies; consumer→provider.**

| Consumer | Provider | Relationship kind | Justification |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Registry | Metadata | Required descriptive contract | Index edition-specific values. |
| Knowledge Graph | Document Identity | Required identity contract | Key logical document nodes. |
| Knowledge Graph | Relationships | Required relationship contract | Interpret typed edges and their provenance. |
| Workflow | Metadata / Policies | Required descriptive/governance contracts | Interpret state and permitted transitions. |
| Baselines | Document Identity / Metadata | Required edition-reference contracts | Select and preserve exact document editions. |
<!-- end-view -->

The selected intended contract dependencies replace the unlabeled Metadata→Registry→Knowledge Graph→Baselines chain. They do not imply a required Registry→Knowledge Graph→Baselines execution sequence or a mandatory Discovery service dependency for snapshot selection. Exact editions and verification evidence can be supplied under the relevant contracts.

A full mandatory graph requires reconciliation with ARC-003/004/005 and the affected component specifications. Do not claim a verified global DAG here; do not conceal a genuine mandatory cycle by changing its edge label. Where the current sources differ, record the conflict and reconcile the responsible source during its scheduled cycle. Referencing a component specification from this Foundation overview is a documentary authority reference, not an execution dependency of Foundation on an upper-layer service.
